summary: Describes a Uniform Resource Name (URN) namespace for naming XML formats and protocols that extend XMPP, when those are defined in specifications published by the XMPP Standards Foundation. It gives such extensions stable, unique names. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Every extra feature for a chat system needs a unique name tag so nobody mixes them up. This note creates the system for making those name tags.

questions: what is the xmpp urn namespace
why use urns instead of http urls
how do xmpp extensions get assigned names
subtitle: A permanent naming system for additions to the XMPP messaging protocol

tldr.problem: XMPP extensions (additions to the core messaging protocol) were named using HTTP URLs, but these can become unreliable if domain control changes, threatening the permanence of extension names.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers a Uniform Resource Name (URN) namespace identifier "xmpp" that gives XMPP extensions stable, permanent names like urn:xmpp:pubsub or urn:xmpp:muc:user, managed by the XMPP Standards Foundation's registrar.
tldr.outcome: XMPP extensions now have durable, reliable names independent of any single domain, improving interoperability and persistence.

today: RFC 4854 is an informational RFC that registered the "xmpp" URN namespace with IANA. It has not been obsoleted. The XMPP Standards Foundation continues to maintain the registry and assign URNs to new extensions as they are standardized.

sections.title: Extensions to a Messaging Protocol
sections.content:
XMPP (Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol) is a real-time messaging and chat protocol, the basis for Jabber and other services. The protocol itself provides basic messaging and presence (online status), but its design is modular: it is fundamentally a way to stream XML data, so developers can add virtually any structured information as extensions.

These extensions are numerous. Some add file transfer, others add multi-user chat or publish-subscribe systems. Each extension needs a unique XML namespace name—a label that identifies what kind of data is inside an XMPP message.

Historically, XMPP extensions used namespace names like http://jabber.org/protocol/pubsub (for a publish-subscribe extension). These are HTTP URLs, which are permanent as long as the domain jabber.org remains under control of the XMPP community. But domain control can change, URLs can become unreachable, and the semantics are tied to an external authority. This document registers a better solution: a Uniform Resource Name (URN) namespace that gives XMPP extensions permanent, unique identifiers.
sections.eli5: XMPP is a chat system that lets people add features like group chats or file transfer. Each feature needs a unique name so messages using that feature are recognized correctly. The old names were web addresses, which could become unreliable.

sections.title: What is a URN?
sections.content:
A Uniform Resource Name (URN) is an identifier with a specific syntax defined in RFC 2141. Unlike a URL, which points to a location on the web, a URN is a persistent, location-independent name for a resource. A URN consists of three parts:

urn: (the scheme), NID (Namespace ID, like "xmpp"), and NSS (Namespace Specific String, like "pubsub").

Examples: urn:isbn:0451450523 identifies a book; urn:xmpp:pubsub (after registration by this RFC) identifies the XMPP publish-subscribe extension.

The key advantage of URNs is permanence and independence. An ISBN number for a book remains the same no matter which bookstore sells it; a URN for an XMPP extension remains the same no matter which organization controls a domain. URNs are managed by registrars responsible for ensuring uniqueness and persistence within their namespace, without depending on DNS or any commercial domain.
sections.eli5: A URN is a permanent ID like a Social Security number, not a location like a home address. Once assigned, it never changes and does not depend on any website.

sections.title: The "xmpp" Namespace Registration
sections.content:
This RFC registers the URN Namespace ID "xmpp" for XMPP extensions and XML formats defined in specifications published by the XMPP Standards Foundation (XSF). The XSF is the standards body behind XMPP.

The structure of XMPP URNs is simple: urn:xmpp:{ShortName}:{SubName}. The ShortName is required and identifies the protocol or format (e.g., "pubsub" for publish-subscribe, "muc" for multi-user chat). The SubName is optional and identifies a particular subset or variant (e.g., "urn:xmpp:muc:user" for the user profile aspect of multi-user chat).

The XSF's XMPP Registrar function manages assignment of all ShortName and SubName strings, maintaining a public registry at the XSF website. This is the same registrar that previously assigned HTTP URL namespaces; it simply shifts to assigning URNs with the same process. Each registered URN is unique and permanent, never reassigned.

New XMPP extensions are only assigned URNs when the relevant extension specification reaches a standard status ("Draft") in the XSF's standards process. This ensures that only formally reviewed extensions receive URNs.
sections.eli5: XMPP extensions get names like "urn:xmpp:pubsub" or "urn:xmpp:muc:user". The XMPP Standards Foundation keeps track of all these names and makes sure no two extensions get the same name.

sections.title: Why URNs Are Better Than HTTP URLs
sections.content:
The shift from HTTP URL-based names to URN-based names solves several problems. First, permanence: an HTTP URL namespace like "http://jabber.org/protocol/..." depends on the jabber.org domain remaining under XSF control. If that domain were lost, sold, or transferred, the namespace URLs would become unreliable or meaningless. A URN, once registered, persists regardless of domain changes or domain transfers.

Second, clarity of intent. An HTTP URL looks like it might point to a web page describing the extension; in reality, it is just an opaque identifier. A URN makes it clear that this is a permanent, universal identifier, not a web address.

Third, separation from IETF standards. XMPP extensions developed by the XSF are distinct from the core XMPP specifications standardized by the IETF (which use IETF URNs like "urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:xmpp-*"). The separate "xmpp" namespace makes this distinction clear.

Finally, independence from any single authority. XMPP extensions are managed by the XSF, an independent standards organization. Using IETF namespaces would imply IETF governance; using a dedicated "xmpp" namespace preserves XSF independence.
sections.eli5: If an extension's name is a web address, it depends on that website staying online. A permanent ID number (URN) never depends on a website, making it more reliable.

sections.title: How the System Works Today
sections.content:
The XMPP Registrar manages a public registry of all assigned XMPP URNs, published at the XSF website. When someone proposes a new XMPP extension (submitted as an XMPP Extension Protocol or XEP specification), it goes through the XSF's open standards process: submitted to an editor, reviewed by the XSF Council, and advanced through stages (Experimental, Proposed, Draft, Final). Once an extension reaches Draft status, the XMPP Registrar assigns it a URN within the "xmpp" tree.

The registrar checks all proposed ShortNames and SubNames against the existing registry to ensure uniqueness. Developers and operators can look up extension names and their specifications on the XSF website, making it easy to discover which extensions are available and which versions are standardized.

For XML documents and data structures that use XMPP extensions, the namespace declaration in the XML simply references the URN (e.g., xmlns='urn:xmpp:pubsub'), making it clear which standardized extension applies. Tools and libraries can recognize these URNs without needing to fetch anything from the web.
sections.eli5: When a new XMPP add-on gets approved, the XSF Registrar assigns it a URN name and adds it to a public list. Anyone building a chat program can look up that name to find out what the feature does.
